sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: Deep learning-based 3D dose prediction boosts radiotherapy planning efficiency and consistency, yet most models rely solely on anatomical data and assume homogeneous beam configurations, impairing their robustness in esophageal cancer intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) with heterogeneous beam arrangements. This study explored whether explicit beam geometry modeling enhances voxel-level dose prediction accuracy, robustness in rare beam configurations, and clinical workflow efficiency.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A retrospective analysis was performed on 751 esophageal cancer IMRT patients. Two models with the identical AS-NeSt backbone were constructed: an anatomy-only dose prediction model (ADP) and an anatomy-and-angle-based model (AADP) integrating ray-tracing-derived beam geometry representations (normalized beam coverage and overlap maps) accessible in pre-planning. Model performance was assessed on an independent test set (n = 100), a rare-beam configuration cohort (n = 33) and a clinical validation cohort (n = 42), against clinical plans as the reference baseline. Evaluation was based on dosimetric metrics and isodose spatial similarity, along with an analysis of its robustness on unseen beam configurations and impact in a crossover clinical workflow study.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Compared with ADP, AADP significantly reduced prediction errors for most targets and organs at risk, cutting average dosimetric error from 2.88% to 2.02%, with prominent improvements in low-to-intermediate dose regions (lung and heart). The mean Dice similarity coefficient of isodose volumes rose from 0.90 to 0.93. For rare beam configurations, AADP exhibited superior robustness (average error: 3.08% vs. 4.52%). Notably, AADP-assisted planning shortened total planning time by up to 65% (from 111.4 to 38.5 min for junior physicists), reduced iterations, and improved intra- and inter-physicist dose consistency.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study confirms explicit ray-tracing-based beam geometry modeling enhances the accuracy, robustness, and clinical utility of 3D dose prediction for esophageal cancer IMRT, supporting beam geometry as a critical component of clinically deployable, physics-informed dose prediction models.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Radiotherapy plays a central role in the management of esophageal cancer. Treatment planning for esophageal cancer remains challenging because the target is often elongated and irregular, and is anatomically close to critical organs at risk (OARs) such as the lungs, heart, and spinal cord. In addition, clinical practice frequently involves complex prescription strategies, including simultaneous integrated boost (SIB), which further increases planning difficulty. These factors make dose distributions highly sensitive to beam configuration and optimization strategies, resulting in iterative trial-and-error planning, prolonged planning time, and inter-planner variability in plan quality [1–3].

To improve efficiency and consistency, automated planning methods have been widely explored. Knowledge-based planning (KBP) and objective-based planning (OBP) leverage prior plans to predict dose-volume histogram (DVH) constraints or optimization objectives, thereby reducing manual tuning and improving reproducibility [3–11]. However, DVHs provide only one-dimensional statistical summaries and cannot characterize the spatial distribution of dose, including intratarget heterogeneity, spatial gradients near OARs, or low- and intermediate-dose spillage into unsegmented regions. This limitation is particularly relevant for thoracic sites such as esophageal cancer, where clinically meaningful differences often arise from spatial dose patterns rather than DVH summaries alone.

Deep learning has enabled voxel-level three-dimensional (3D) dose prediction as an alternative that directly models spatial dose distributions. Prior studies using 3D convolutional architectures have demonstrated promising performance across multiple disease sites [12–16]. In our previous work, asymmetric ResNeSt (AS-NeSt) model was developed for esophageal cancer radiotherapy dose prediction under multi-prescription settings and was shown to improve spatial agreement and planning workflow efficiency [17].

Nevertheless, an important limitation emerges when such models are deployed in real-world practice. Many existing dose prediction approaches are anatomy-driven and implicitly assume that beam configurations are fixed or similar between training and testing cohorts. In contrast, routine esophageal intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) often involves heterogeneous beam configurations—patient-specific variations in beam number and orientation driven by anatomical constraints, lung/heart sparing requirements, and institutional or planner-dependent strategies [13, 18–21]. Under such heterogeneity, anatomy-only models can become unstable, especially in low- and intermediate-dose regions that are strongly governed by beam directions and cumulative beam overlap rather than target geometry alone [22].

The physical dependence of thoracic dose deposition on beam orientation makes this issue especially prominent. Small changes in beam angles can substantially alter lung low- and intermediate-dose exposure, anterior-posterior arrangements can affect cardiac dose, and target dose gradients depend on multi-beam superposition [22]. Several studies have incorporated beam-related information into dose prediction and reported improved robustness compared with anatomy-only approaches [18, 19, 23, 24]. However, such studies remain scarce in complex tumors such as esophageal cancer, and systematic validation under clinically realistic and rare beam configurations, as well as evaluation of downstream clinical workflow impact, remain limited.

Therefore, this study investigates whether explicitly modeling beam geometry can improve the robustness of pre-planning 3D dose prediction for esophageal cancer radiotherapy under clinically realistic beam heterogeneity. We propose an anatomical and angle-based dose prediction (AADP) framework that integrates ray-tracing-derived beam geometry features with anatomical structure information, introducing a simple and physically interpretable beam encoding that is available at the pre-planning stage. By explicitly incorporating beam-directional information, this work aims to address a key limitation of anatomy-only dose prediction models and to establish a more robust and clinically relevant paradigm for voxel-level dose prediction in esophageal IMRT.

sec.title: Design overview
sec.p: This study evaluated whether explicit incorporation of beam geometry information improves pre-planning 3D dose prediction and provides practical benefits in clinical radiotherapy workflows.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, retrospective radiotherapy planning data were collected and processed. Patient selection, cohort construction, and study grouping are described in section “Patient cohort and study design”, and treatment planning details are provided in section “Treatment planning and beam configuration”. Two deep learning-based dose prediction models were constructed for comparison: an anatomy-only dose prediction model (ADP) and the proposed AADP model incorporating both anatomical and beam geometry information. The dose prediction framework is described in section “The dose prediction framework”. Model performance was assessed in terms of dosimetric accuracy, spatial similarity of dose distributions, and robustness under rare beam configuration scenarios section “Evaluation strategy”. In addition, a clinical workflow efficiency study was conducted to evaluate the impact of model-assisted dose prediction on treatment planning efficiency and consistency section “Clinical workflow efficiency evaluation”.

sec.title: Patient cohort and study design
sec.p: This retrospective study was approved by the institutional review board of our institution (IRB No. KS 24254). The requirement for written informed consent was waived owing to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of fully anonymized data.

Patients treated with radiotherapy for esophageal cancer between June 2015 and June 2024 at our institution and a collaborating center were screened for eligibility. Inclusion criteria were: (1) pathologically confirmed esophageal cancer; (2) treatment with IMRT; (3) availability of complete planning data, including planning computed tomography (CT) images, structure sets, beam configurations, and clinically approved dose distributions. Patients with incomplete or missing planning information were excluded.

According to the study objectives, a total of 751 eligible patients were allocated into four non-overlapping cohorts: (1) a model development cohort of 576 patients (500 for training and 76 for validation); (2) an independent test cohort of 100 patients (50 from our institution and 50 from a collaborating center); (3) a rare-beam configuration cohort of 33 patients for generalization evaluation; and (4) a clinical workflow efficiency evaluation cohort of 42 patients. All patient identifiers were removed prior to data processing and analysis.

sec.title: Treatment planning and beam configuration
sec.p: All patients were treated with IMRT plans generated using the auto-planning module of the Pinnacle treatment planning system (TPS; version 9.10, Philips Radiation Oncology Systems, Fitchburg, WI, USA) with 6-MV photon beams. Each treatment plan consisted of 4–9 fields. Beam angles were selected by experienced medical physicists based on tumor location, patient anatomy, and OAR sparing requirements. The distribution of beam numbers covered both commonly used clinical configurations and less frequent, patient-specific arrangements. Beam orientations varied substantially among patients, reflecting real-world clinical practice and resulting in heterogeneous beam-angle patterns. All plans met institutional dose constraints and were reviewed and approved by attending radiation oncologists prior to treatment.

sec.title: The dose prediction framework
sec.p: ADP model and the proposed AADP model were developed in this study. The two models share an identical network backbone, training strategy, and loss function, and differ only in the inclusion of explicit beam geometry representations in AADP.

An overview of the proposed AADP framework is shown in Fig. 2. The input representation consists of anatomical structure channels and, in AADP, additional beam geometry channels derived from ray-tracing-based encoding, as described in section “Input representation and data preprocessing discussion”. These inputs are processed by a deep neural network based on the AS-NeSt architecture [17] section “Network architecture” to generate a single-channel 3D dose distribution.

caption.p: Overview of the anatomical and angle-based dose prediction (AADP) framework. Anatomical structure masks and ray-tracing-derived beam geometry representations are jointly encoded as multi-channel inputs and processed by the AS-NeSt-based deep neural network to generate a 3D dose distribution

sec.title: Input representation and data preprocessing
sec.p: Consistent with our previous work [17], anatomical information was encoded using multi-channel 3D binary masks. The planning target volume (PTV) and OARs were provided as independent channels.

Specifically, one channel represented the PTV mask. For patients with one or two targets, voxel values within the PTV channel were assigned the corresponding prescription dose, thereby jointly encoding target geometry and prescription information. Four additional channels represented the heart, spinal cord, lungs, and body contour, respectively. Voxels outside all regions of interest (ROIs) were labeled as background.

sec.p: This ray-tracing [25, 26]-based representation is not intended to approximate physical dose deposition or beam modulation. Instead, it provides a coarse, voxel-level encoding of beam directional exposure and overlap patterns that are available at the pre-planning stage. As illustrated in Fig. 3, beam-direction information was explicitly incorporated using a ray-tracing-based beam geometry encoding strategy. First, a ray-tracing technology was employed to determine the radiation paths of individual beams through the patient anatomy. (i) ray-voxel intersection, (ii) normalized beam coverage, and (iii) threshold-based beam overlap maps.

The normalized beam coverage map and the derived overlap masks were concatenated with the anatomical channels to form the final multi-channel network input.

sec.title: Network architecture
sec.p: As in Fig. 2 shown, the proposed framework is built upon the AS-NeSt architecture [17] previously developed by our group. AS-NeSt is based on a 3D U-Net backbone and incorporates 3D ResNeSt blocks as its core components.

Each ResNeSt block employs a split-attention mechanism that groups feature channels and applies adaptive attention weighting within cardinal groups, enabling effective multi-scale spatial feature aggregation. The network adopts an asymmetric encoder-decoder design, consisting of four encoding stages and two decoding stages, connected via skip connections to preserve spatial context.

In this study, the original AS-NeSt architecture was extended by expanding the input channel dimension to accommodate the beam geometry features described above. The network outputs a single-channel 3D dose distribution.

sec.title: Model training and implementation details
sec.p: Both AADP and ADP models were trained under identical conditions to ensure a fair comparison. Training was performed using the Adam optimizer on two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The learning rate was set to 1*10− 4, the batch size was 2, and training was conducted for 400 epochs.

sec.title: Evaluation strategy
sec.p: Model performance was evaluated from dosimetric accuracy, spatial similarity, robustness to rare beam configurations, and clinical workflow impact.

sec.title: Dosimetric metrics
sec.p: Dosimetric accuracy was evaluated using standard PTV and OAR metrics, including the doses received by 2%, 95%, 98%, and 99% of the PTV volume (D2, D95, D98, D99), conformity index (CI), homogeneity index (HI), mean dose (Dmean), maximum dose (Dmax), and OAR-specific percentage volume receiving over x Gy (Vx). The CI and HI formulas can be found in supplementary materials. A complete list of evaluated metrics is provided in Table 1.

sec.title: Spatial similarity metrics
Rare beam configuration evaluation
sec.p: To assess generalization performance, a subset of 33 patients with beam configurations that were rare and absent from the training set was evaluated separately. Rare beam configurations were defined as beam number-angle combinations not observed during training and whose beam-angle distributions deviated from the dominant patterns in the training cohort, as verified by histogram-based comparisons of beam number and angular spacing.

sec.title: Clinical workflow efficiency evaluation
sec.p: A clinical workflow efficiency study was conducted with a cross-over design involving 42 patients, a junior physicist (1 year of experience), a senior physicist (5 + years of experience), and an attending radiation oncologist (10 + years of experience). To minimize biases from case heterogeneity and individual experience, model-predicted 3D dose distributions were alternately provided (model-assisted group) or withheld (control group) prior to plan optimization for two 21-case groups (Group A and Group B), with roles exchanged after a three-month washout period (Fig. 4 (A)). For the model-assisted group, AADP-predicted dose distributions served as pre-optimization references to guide beam selection and plan refinement (Fig. 4 (B)).

Planning efficiency and plan consistency were evaluated by recording core metrics throughout the planning process (from initiation to final approval). Planning efficiency was designed to evaluate the AADP model’s auxiliary effect on the speed of clinical workflows, while plan consistency aimed to assess whether disparities in treatment plan quality caused by differences in physicists’ clinical experience could be mitigated with the assistance of the AADP model. Efficiency metrics included physician-physicist interaction count, plan revision iterations, and total planning time. Plan consistency was quantified by following two key indices. Intra-physicist dose difference: the average relative variation in key dosimetric metrics (Table 1) for the same patient between a physicist’s initial draft plan and final approved plan; Inter-physicist dose difference: the average relative disparity in key dosimetric metrics for the same patient between the independently approved plans of the junior and senior physicists.
All consistency metrics were normalized to the percentage of prescription dose (dose values) or organ volume (volume-based metrics) for cross-case and cross-metric comparability.

caption.p: Experimental design (A) and Clinical workflow (B) for beam selection and treatment planning assisted by the AADP model. The predicted 3D dose distribution generated by the AADP model is provided prior to plan optimization to guide beam selection and planning refinement, thereby reducing planning iterations and improving workflow efficiency

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Paired t-tests were used for statistical comparisons when normality assumptions were satisfied. Otherwise, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was applied. A two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Patient characteristics
sec.p: Baseline characteristics of development set, test set and other set are summarized in Table 2. The three cohorts were well balanced with respect to age, sex, histology, clinical stage, tumor location, target volume, chemotherapy receipt, and prescription regimen. Squamous cell carcinoma was the predominant histology, and most patients presented with stage III disease. Tumors were most commonly located in the middle thoracic esophagus.

Regarding beam configuration, plans ranged from 4 to 9 fields across all cohorts, with four-beam arrangements being the most frequent and nine-beam setups the least common. The distribution of beam numbers was comparable across cohorts, reflecting routine clinical personalization of beam arrangements to balance target coverage and thoracic OAR sparing.

sec.title: Overall performance of dose prediction models with and without beam inputs
Training convergence and computational efficiency
sec.p: The hyperparameters for ADP model and the proposed AADP model are summarized in Table 3. Despite incorporating explicit beam-direction information, the AADP model introduced only a negligible increase in trainable parameters (35.68 M vs. 35.68 M). During validation, the AADP model achieved substantially lower loss values, with the best mean squared error (MSE) reduced from 11.41 to 7.25 and the mean absolute error (MAE) reduced from 1.34 to 1.01 compared with the ADP model (Fig. 5).

Importantly, inference efficiency was preserved, with comparable prediction times for AADP and ADP (6.74 ms vs. 6.69 ms per case), indicating that the performance gains were achieved without additional computational burden.

sec.title: Comparison of dose distributions and DVHs
sec.p: Representative comparisons between clinical dose distributions and predicted doses from the AADP and ADP models are illustrated in Fig. 6(A). Both models successfully reproduced the overall spatial dose patterns of the clinical plans; however, the AADP model demonstrated visibly reduced discrepancies, particularly in low- and intermediate-dose regions.

DVH comparisons (Fig. 6(B)) further confirmed these observations. While both models showed good agreement with clinical DVHs for PTV and OARs, the AADP model consistently yielded closer alignment across dose ranges, especially for lung and heart structures.

(A) Representative axial dose distributions for the clinical plan, AADP prediction, ADP prediction, and corresponding dose difference maps. (B) Dose-volume histograms (DVHs) comparing the clinical dose (solid lines) with predicted doses from the AADP (dotted lines) and ADP (dashed lines) models

sec.title: Errors in mean and maximum dose prediction
sec.p: The absolute prediction errors for Dmean and Dmax across all structures are summarized in Table 4 and visualized in Fig. 7.

For the PTV, the AADP model achieved significantly lower prediction errors in both Dmean and Dmax compared with the ADP model (P < 0.05). Specifically, the mean absolute errors for PTV Dmean and Dmax were reduced from 4.31% to 3.70% and from 1.01% to 0.79% of the prescription dose, respectively. For organs at risk, notable reductions were observed for bilateral lungs, total lung, and body dose predictions. Although the reduction in spinal cord mean dose was not statistically significant, the AADP model achieved a significantly lower prediction error for spinal cord Dmax (P = 0.044). Conversely, no significant difference was observed between the two models for heart Dmax, whereas the prediction error for heart mean dose (HMD) was significantly reduced with AADP.

Overall, when averaged across all evaluated structures, the AADP model yielded lower prediction errors for both Dmean (3.17% vs. 3.72%) and Dmax (1.04% vs. 1.50%), demonstrating improved robustness and consistency relative to the anatomy-only model.

sec.title: Comparison of dosimetric metrics
sec.p: A detailed comparison of dose-volume and dosimetric prediction errors is presented in Table 5.

For target-related metrics, the AADP model significantly reduced errors in D2, Dmax, Dmean, with reductions up to approximately 1% of the prescription dose (all P < 0.05). The CI was also lower with the AADP model (4.73 × 10⁻² vs. 5.93 × 10⁻²). No significant differences were observed for D95, D98, D99, or HI. For OAR metrics, the most pronounced improvements were observed in low-dose lung parameters. Specifically, errors in V5 for total lung, right lung, and left lung were reduced by more than 2% compared with the ADP model (all P < 0.001). Moderate but significant reductions were also observed for lung V20, mean lung dose (MLD), heart V30/V40, mean heart dose (MHD), and Spinal cord D2/Dmax.
Across all evaluated metrics, the average prediction error decreased from 2.88% with ADP to 2.02% with AADP.

sec.title: Isodose volume similarity

caption.p: Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) for isodose volume predictions on the conventional test set. (A) DSC curves for the AADP model, showing individual patients (dashed lines) and the cohort mean (solid black line). (B) Corresponding DSC curves for the ADP model. (C) DSC differences between the AADP and ADP models (AADP-ADP) across isodose levels

sec.p: Spatial agreement between predicted and clinical dose distributions was quantified using DSC, as shown in Fig. 8.

Both models achieved high DSC values across isodose levels; however, the AADP model consistently outperformed the ADP model. The mean DSC in the test set was 0.93 for AADP compared with 0.90 for ADP, corresponding to an average improvement of 3.49%.

The largest DSC gains were observed in low-dose regions (≤ 10% isodose), where improvements exceeded 5%. Additionally, the narrower variability band of the AADP curves indicates improved inter-patient consistency.

sec.title: Performance on unseen rare beam configurations
sec.p: In the Unseen-Rare Beam Test Set, both models exhibited increased prediction errors compared with the conventional test set; however, the degradation was substantially smaller for the AADP model.

As summarized in Table 6, the average prediction error increased from 2.02% to 3.08% for AADP, compared with an increase from 2.88% to 4.52% for ADP. The performance gap between models widened from 0.86% to 1.44%. Notably, low-dose lung metrics showed error reductions exceeding 3% with AADP.

Furthermore, dose metrics that were not significantly different in the conventional test set (e.g., D98 and D99) became significantly improved in favor of AADP under rare-beam conditions. In contrast, spinal cord dose predictions showed no significant difference between models.

DSC analysis (Fig. 9) demonstrated that the AADP model achieved a mean DSC of 0.87 in the Unseen-Rare Beam Test Set, representing a 9.49% improvement over the ADP model(0.79), substantially larger than that observed under conventional test set.

sec.title: Clinical workflow efficiency
sec.p: The impact of AADP-assisted planning on clinical workflow efficiency is summarized in Table 7.

For junior physicists, the number of physician-physicist interactions, plan revisions, and total planning time were reduced by 55.20%, 59.68%, and 65.40%, respectively (all P < 0.001). Average planning time decreased from 111.41 min to 38.54 min. Dose variability within physicists was reduced by 64.29%.

Senior physicists also demonstrated significant improvements, although with smaller relative reductions. Importantly, inter-physicist dose difference decreased by 80.58% after introducing the AADP model, indicating a substantial improvement in planning consistency across experience levels.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Building upon prior work on three-dimensional dose prediction using anatomical information alone, the present study further addresses a key clinical characteristic of esophageal cancer radiotherapy: highly individualized beam configurations and pronounced inter-planner variability. To this end, we explicitly incorporated beam-angle geometric information and constructed a voxel-wise representation of beam penetration and overlap patterns via ray tracing. Based on this design, we proposed an AADP model that integrates both anatomical structures and beam geometry for 3D dose prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with the anatomy-driven ADP model, AADP consistently improves overall dosimetric accuracy and spatial agreement. These gains are particularly evident at target boundaries, within low-to-intermediate dose spill regions, and under testing scenarios featuring highly heterogeneous beam settings, including rare or previously unseen configurations. Importantly, such performance improvements are expected to translate into tangible workflow benefits, including fewer planning iterations, reduced planning time, and mitigated inter-planner dose variability, thereby providing more actionable guidance for pre-treatment planning decision support.

sec.title: Clinical rationale and methodological value of introducing beam-angle information
sec.p: From a clinical workflow perspective, beam-angle information is not a post-treatment outcome variable; rather, it is a geometric parameter that can be preliminarily determined after CT simulation and target delineation, based on tumor location, anatomy, and clinical experience, before entering dose optimization and modulation. Therefore, beam-angle information can be regarded as a critical intermediate variable linking patient anatomy to the final dose distribution, enabling realistic opportunities for dose prediction and toxicity assessment in the pre-optimization stage.

From a radiophysical standpoint, the 3D dose distribution is jointly determined by anatomical heterogeneity, beam directions, path superposition, and subsequent optimization/modulation. Anatomy-only prediction frameworks may perform well when beam arrangements are relatively standardized, but they implicitly assume that beam geometry patterns remain consistent between training and testing. When testing cases deviate from dominant patterns in the training set—due to differences across institutions, planners, beam numbers, or angular distributions—pure anatomy-driven models tend to exhibit prediction bias, particularly in beam-path-sensitive low-dose spill regions and global spatial morphology reconstruction [18, 22, 28].

The proposed ray-tracing–based beam representation is physically interpretable. Its purpose is not to approximate the final modulation outcome, but rather to encode coarse beam penetration pathways and multi-beam overlap patterns within the patient. This representation offers several advantages: (1) it preserves directional propagation cues, facilitating identification of low-dose spread; (2) overlap of multiple beams naturally manifests as high-density regions in the feature map, consistent with the dose superposition mechanism; and (3) it does not rely on dose calculation results, avoiding information leakage. With this voxel-level, direction-aware geometric input channel, the model can simultaneously learn complementary mappings of anatomy-to-dose and beam-to-dose, yielding more pronounced improvements in geometric consistency, particularly in complex dose regions formed by multi-beam path interactions. Collectively, these findings support the notion that injecting interpretable physical priors into deep learning models can mitigate instability on out-of-distribution samples and improve robustness and clinical deployability.

sec.title: Why beam information is particularly important for esophageal IMRT
sec.p: In esophageal IMRT, beam configuration heterogeneity is not an edge case, but a natural consequence of thoracic anatomical complexity and stringent OAR sparing priorities. Beam number and direction often require adjustment to balance target coverage against lung and heart protection, and substantial differences exist across planners and institutions. Consequently, when beam arrangement is unspecified, the mapping from anatomy to dose distribution is not unique. This non-uniqueness is most prominent in low- and intermediate-dose regions, which depend strongly on beam directions and overlap patterns. Anatomy-only models may effectively learn an “average beam effect” from the training distribution, leading to performance degradation when testing cases deviate from dominant beam patterns [18, 22, 28]. The robustness gain of AADP observed in external datasets and under rare/unseen beam configurations is consistent with this mechanism.

sec.title: Comparison with prior beam-related dose prediction studies
sec.p: Multiple studies have highlighted the importance of incorporating beam information for robust dose prediction. Barragán-Montero et al. explicitly investigated heterogeneous beam arrangements in lung IMRT and showed that including beam setup information improves robustness, especially in low- and intermediate-dose regions that are sensitive to beam layout [18]. Zhou et al. developed a beam-aware 3D dose prediction framework for postoperative rectal cancer IMRT, demonstrating improved consistency when a beam configuration matrix is used as input compared with anatomy-only models [19]. Peng et al. systematically examined the effects of beam angle, beam number, and patient setup on cervical cancer IMRT dose prediction, emphasizing that beam variability can substantially impact model performance and motivating explicit beam modeling strategies [29]. Beyond configuration-aware inputs, other research directions include modeling beam controllability or decomposition, such as Pareto/adjustable dose prediction frameworks and per-beam dose decomposition approaches that highlight individual beam contributions and controllable trade-offs [23, 30, 31].

Overall, these studies establish a consistent theme: explicit beam information enhances robustness when beam arrangements vary. The present study differs in two practical aspects. First, we focus on esophageal cancer, where elongated targets and strict thoracic OAR constraints induce clinically realistic heterogeneity, including rare/unseen configurations. Second, our ray-tracing encoding provides a voxel-level, physically interpretable representation of beam traversal characteristics that is available in the pre-planning stage and does not require fluence maps, monitor units, or MLC sequences. This design preserves clinical practicality while introducing a meaningful physics-informed inductive bias. Notably, the proposed representation does not aim to approximate final modulation, but rather to encode directional exposure patterns to help resolve the inherently complex mapping between beam configuration and 3D dose distribution. By learning from large-scale clinical cases, the network implicitly captures voxel-wise correspondences between beam traversal and dose deposition, without requiring simulated or precomputed dose distributions as input. The observed robustness gains indicate that even coarse yet interpretable beam geometry features can provide substantial inductive bias for voxel-level dose prediction, particularly in low- and intermediate-dose regions.

sec.title: Clinical implications of improved low-dose region prediction
sec.p: A key finding of this study is that beam-angle information yields particularly notable improvements in low-to-intermediate lung dose regions (e.g., V5 and V20), accompanied by more pronounced gains in spatial consistency. This observation is clinically meaningful. In esophageal radiotherapy, the spatial distribution of low-dose lung exposure is highly dependent on beam orientation and beam number, and low-dose exposure characteristics are closely associated with dose-limiting toxicities such as RP [32, 33] Anatomy-only models struggle to robustly capture the “low-dose bath” effect driven by beam traversal pathways, leading to biases in both volume-based metrics and spatial morphology. By integrating beam geometry features, AADP more plausibly reconstructs beam-contributed low-dose coverage patterns, thereby enhancing prediction stability and clinical credibility.

Therefore, incorporating beam-angle information not only improves dose prediction performance itself, but also establishes a critical foundation for downstream applications where predicted dose distributions are used for pre-treatment toxicity risk assessment. This is particularly relevant for RP risk modeling, where low-dose dosimetric features often serve as key predictors. Furthermore, emerging research in dosiomics, radiomics, and multi-omics integration highlights the importance of dose spatial descriptors for toxicity prediction; thus, improved reconstruction of low-dose regions is expected to directly impact the reliability and transferability of such models [34–36].

sec.title: Significance and boundaries of robustness improvement (gain-on-demand rather than universal replacement)
sec.p: Under highly heterogeneous beam settings, AADP demonstrates stronger robustness than ADP. This suggests that when test cases deviate from common beam patterns in the training set, explicit beam geometry provides crucial contextual information and reduces reliance on implicit planning-style priors, thereby improving generalization. This property is essential for real-world deployment, since clinical beam arrangements are not standardized across institutions and can vary substantially even among planners within the same institution.

However, our findings also indicate that the value of beam-angle information is conditional. In scenarios where beam configurations are relatively regular, the training set sufficiently covers beam patterns, and beam geometry remains stable, anatomy-only models may already satisfy baseline prediction needs, and the incremental gain from beam-angle features may be limited. In other words, beam information is better viewed as an enhancement source that improves performance in challenging cases (high beam heterogeneity, insufficient training coverage, pronounced domain shift) and in tasks requiring accurate reconstruction of low-dose regions (e.g., toxicity risk assessment), rather than universally replacing anatomy as the core input. This “gain-on-demand” characteristic may guide future decisions regarding model complexity control, deployment strategy, and resource investment.

It is also worth noting that anatomy-only models often maintain strong accuracy in high-dose regions. This is largely due to the strong constraints imposed by prescription and target coverage requirements in IMRT planning: high-dose regions are intentionally confined and shaped within the PTV to meet conformity and coverage objectives, resulting in lower variability across beam configurations. Thus, target geometry and prescription information—already encoded in anatomy-only inputs—may suffice to approximate the dominant shape of high-dose distributions. In contrast, low- and intermediate-dose regions more directly reflect cumulative effects of beam-path traversal through heterogeneous anatomy and are highly sensitive to beam directions and overlap patterns, making them difficult to uniquely infer from anatomy alone [18, 29]. The observed improvements in lung V5/V20 and thoracic OAR dose metrics under AADP are consistent with this interpretation.

sec.title: Workflow implications: from retrospective accuracy to pre-planning decision support
sec.p: An important contribution of this study is that it goes beyond retrospective dosimetric evaluation to consider downstream workflow impact. If reliable 3D predicted dose distributions can be provided in the pre-optimization phase, model outputs may support early beam selection and guide subsequent dose optimization, thereby reducing repetitive interactions and plan revisions. The observed reductions in planning time and inter-planner dose variability suggest that beam-aware dose prediction can serve as an actionable pre-treatment decision-support tool, rather than merely a retrospective benchmark. In particular, reduced inter-planner variability implies that predicted dose distributions can help standardize early planning decisions and reduce subjective differences, improving planning consistency and efficiency—aligning with broader discussions on clinical acceptability and automation value in AI-assisted radiotherapy planning.

sec.title: Limitations and future directions
sec.p: Despite the clear performance gains, several limitations should be acknowledged and warrant further investigation. First, the current beam representation remains limited in its expressiveness. Our beam encoding primarily captures beam angles and geometric traversal paths, without incorporating modulation-related information such as beam weights, fluence maps, MLC sequences/dynamics, monitor units, or optimization parameters. Consequently, its ability to reproduce local high-dose hotspots, steep gradients, and modulation-dominated dose sculpting is inherently constrained. Future work could explore hierarchical or progressive strategies: starting from coarse beam geometry in the pre-planning stage, and gradually introducing modulation descriptors when available, thereby bridging pre-planning guidance with post-optimization refinement. Second, cross-institution generalization requires larger-scale validation. Although external testing indicates improved robustness, additional validation across more centers, diverse delivery platforms, and broader beam strategy distributions is needed to assess external validity under variations in TPS, dose calculation algorithms, and institutional protocols. Third, direct coupling validation with toxicity risk modeling remains insufficient. While we emphasize the importance of improved low-dose prediction for RP risk assessment, future studies should systematically evaluate the validity of using predicted dose as a substitute for delivered/planned dose in RP risk prediction, and further quantify its incremental contribution within dosiomics/radiomics/multi-omics fusion frameworks. Finally, this study focuses on static dose prediction and does not explicitly consider respiratory motion or adaptive re-planning. Given the thoracic location of esophageal tumors, integrating motion-aware representations or four-dimensional information represents a promising direction to enhance clinical relevance.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Explicit modeling of beam geometry via ray-tracing-derived voxel-level features significantly improves 3D dose prediction for esophageal cancer radiotherapy under heterogeneous and rare beam configurations. Compared with an anatomy-only model, the proposed AADP framework enhances robustness—particularly in low- and intermediate-dose regions—and yields tangible clinical workflow benefits by reducing planning iterations, planning time, and inter-planner variability. These results highlight beam geometry as a critical component for clinically deployable, physics-informed dose prediction and provide a foundation for future extensions to broader modalities, motion-aware scenarios, and adaptive radiotherapy.
